common_name: Cody Buffalograss (Improved Cold-Hardy Seeded Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow cold-treated (stratified) seed at 2-3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft once soil is consistently above 65°F; Cody is a USDA-ARS/University of Nebraska release selected for more uniform seed germination and better fall color retention than older common buffalograss seed sources.

directions: Sow stratified seed into a firm, weed-free seedbed after soil has warmed reliably above 65°F, keeping the surface lightly moist until the stand fills in over several weeks. Cody was bred for more even seedling emergence and improved cold hardiness compared with older common buffalograss seed, making it a more dependable choice for northern Great Plains lawns. Mow occasionally at 3-4 inches or leave unmowed for a soft, informal turf, and expect the stand to need only rainfall in most seasons once roots are established. Avoid rich, acidic, or poorly drained soils, which favor weed competition over this naturally low-input native grass.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

planting.note: Sow cold-treated seed at 2-3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft once soil is reliably above 65°F; Bowie was released alongside Cody from the same USDA-ARS breeding effort and offers similarly improved germination uniformity over unimproved common buffalograss seed.

directions: Sow stratified seed in late spring once soils have warmed past 65°F, watering lightly and frequently until the young stand knits together. Bowie shares its breeding origin with Cody buffalograss, both selected from USDA-ARS and university trials for more reliable seed germination than older common seed lots. Once established it needs only occasional deep watering during prolonged drought and can be mowed at 3-4 inches a few times a season or left unmowed for a prairie-style lawn. It tolerates heat, poor soil fertility, and cold winters well but will not persist in shade or in frequently irrigated, high-fertility turf settings.

planting.note: Establish only from sod or plugs, since Prestige is a vegetatively propagated female selection with little to no viable seed; plant once soil is reliably above 65°F and irrigate consistently until stolons knit together.

directions: Plant plugs or sod sections in full sun once the soil has warmed, spacing plugs closely to speed lateral fill-in by stolons. Prestige is a vegetatively propagated, female-only buffalograss selection bred at the University of Nebraska for finer leaf texture and denser cover than older seeded types, and because it produces little viable seed it stays tidier and less weedy in appearance. Mow occasionally at 2-3 inches for a more finished lawn look or leave it unmowed, and expect it to need supplemental water only during extended summer drought once roots are established. Like all buffalograss it declines in shade and in wet, high-fertility soils, performing best on lean, well-drained ground in full sun.

common_name: UC Verde Buffalograss (Low-Water Vegetative Lawn Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from plugs spaced about 12 inches apart in full sun once soil is reliably above 70°F; UC Verde is a vegetatively propagated selection developed for the hot, dry summers and mild winters of California and the desert Southwest and does not come true from seed.

directions: Set plugs about a foot apart in full sun once summer soil temperatures are consistently warm, and irrigate regularly through the first season while the stolons spread to close the gaps. UC Verde was selected by the University of California, Davis specifically for reliable performance as a low-water lawn substitute in hot-summer, mild-winter climates such as California and the low desert Southwest. Once filled in it needs dramatically less irrigation than cool-season lawns and tolerates infrequent mowing at 3-4 inches or no mowing at all for a soft meadow look. It goes tan and dormant with the first hard frost and is less cold hardy than Great Plains buffalograss selections, so it is best suited to milder winter climates rather than the northern edge of the buffalograss range.

common_name: Bewitched Kentucky Bluegrass (Dark Green Disease-Resistant Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall at 2-3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft into fertile, well-prepared soil; Bewitched is a modern turf-type Kentucky bluegrass cultivar bred for dark color and strong resistance to dollar spot and gray leaf spot, and it can also be sown in early spring where fall seeding is not practical.

directions: Sow into a firm, fertile seedbed in early fall or early spring, keeping the surface consistently moist until germination and early establishment are complete. Bewitched is a newer turf-type Kentucky bluegrass selected for exceptionally dark green color, high shoot density, and strong resistance to dollar spot and gray leaf spot, two diseases that trouble older bluegrass cultivars in humid climates. It spreads by rhizomes to self-repair minor damage and thin spots, but like all Kentucky bluegrasses it goes summer-dormant under prolonged heat and drought stress unless irrigated. It performs best in full sun to very light shade and is frequently blended with perennial ryegrass and fine fescue for a dense, high-quality home lawn.

common_name: Blacksburg Kentucky Bluegrass (Shade-Tolerant Compact Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall at 2-3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft; Blacksburg is a compact-type cultivar released by Virginia Tech noted for good density and better tolerance of light shade than many older Kentucky bluegrass cultivars.

directions: Establish in early fall (or early spring) into a well-prepared, moderately fertile seedbed, watering lightly and often until seedlings are rooted in. Blacksburg is a compact-type Kentucky bluegrass released by Virginia Tech, valued for producing a dense, medium-dark green turf with somewhat better performance in light shade than many older common-type bluegrass seed lines. Like other Kentucky bluegrasses it spreads by rhizomes and can recover from moderate wear, but it still requires supplemental irrigation to avoid summer dormancy during hot, dry stretches. It is commonly blended with other bluegrass cultivars and fine fescue in seed mixes intended for lawns with mixed sun and shade exposure.

common_name: Rugby II Kentucky Bluegrass (Improved Disease-Resistant Sports Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall at 2-3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft; Rugby II is an improved selection from the original Rugby Kentucky bluegrass bred for better density and disease resistance, widely used on athletic fields and high-quality home lawns.

directions: Seed into a firm, fertile bed in early fall or early spring and keep consistently moist through germination and the first few mowings. Rugby II improves on the older Rugby Kentucky bluegrass cultivar with denser tillering and better resistance to common bluegrass diseases, making it a popular choice for athletic fields, parks, and premium home lawns that see regular traffic. It spreads by rhizomes to fill in divots and thin spots over time, but performs best with full sun and consistent moisture, going dormant in extended summer heat without irrigation. Blend it with other elite Kentucky bluegrass cultivars or perennial ryegrass for faster establishment and broader disease coverage in a home lawn seed mix.

planting.note: Sow at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft (or use as a quick overseed) in late summer to early fall; Manhattan 3 is a fine-textured, turf-type perennial ryegrass that germinates faster than any other cool-season lawn grass, often within a week.

directions: Broadcast seed into a well-prepared bed in early fall (or early spring) and keep the surface evenly moist; Manhattan 3 germinates within about a week, faster than Kentucky bluegrass or fescue, making it useful for quick cover and overseeding. It is a fine-bladed, turf-type descendant of the original Manhattan perennial ryegrass, bred for finer texture, better mowing quality, and improved disease resistance than older forage-type ryegrass. It does not spread by rhizomes or stolons, so thin or damaged areas need reseeding rather than natural fill-in, and it is often blended with Kentucky bluegrass to combine fast germination with long-term spreading recovery. Mow regularly at 2-3 inches, provide full sun, and water during dry spells, since perennial ryegrass has a shallower root system than bluegrass or fescue.

common_name: Palmer III Perennial Ryegrass (Dark Green Turf-Type Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall or use as a quick-germinating overseed; Palmer III is the third generation of the Palmer turf-type perennial ryegrass series, selected for dark green color and improved disease resistance over earlier Palmer releases.

directions: Sow into a firm, moist seedbed in early fall or early spring; like other turf-type perennial ryegrasses, Palmer III germinates within about a week under favorable soil temperatures, among the fastest of any lawn grass. It is valued for dark green color, fine leaf texture, and improved resistance to red thread and other common ryegrass diseases compared with earlier Palmer-series releases. As a bunch-type grass it does not spread laterally, so it is most often blended with Kentucky bluegrass or used as a component in high-traffic sports turf mixes rather than grown alone. Provide full sun, regular mowing at 2-3 inches, and supplemental water during dry periods to keep the stand dense and free of gaps.

common_name: Jamestown II Chewings Fescue (Fine-Bladed Shade-Tolerant Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall into lean, well-drained soil; Jamestown II is an improved chewings fescue selected for finer texture and better shade and drought tolerance than the original Jamestown cultivar.

directions: Sow into a lean, well-drained seedbed in early fall, watering to establish and then tapering irrigation once seedlings root in. Jamestown II is an improved bunch-type chewings fescue bred for finer, needle-like leaf texture and better performance in dry shade than the original Jamestown release, making it a mainstay of shade and low-maintenance lawn seed mixes. It tolerates low fertility and infrequent mowing better than Kentucky bluegrass or perennial ryegrass, and can be mowed at 2-3 inches for a conventional lawn or left taller in naturalized, no-mow plantings. It is commonly blended with creeping red fescue, hard fescue, and a small percentage of Kentucky bluegrass for shaded lawn areas where bermudagrass and full-sun cool-season grasses struggle.

common_name: Boreal Creeping Red Fescue (Cold-Hardy Spreading Shade Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall into well-drained soil; Boreal is a strong-rhizome creeping red fescue cultivar developed in Canada for exceptional cold hardiness and reliable spread in short-season northern climates.

directions: Sow into a well-prepared, well-drained seedbed in early fall, keeping the surface moist through germination and early rooting. Boreal is a strong-rhizome creeping red fescue selected in Canada for outstanding winter hardiness, allowing it to persist through harsher cold than many other fine fescues while still forming a fine-textured, shade-tolerant turf. Unlike bunch-type chewings fescue, it spreads slowly by short rhizomes and can knit together thin or damaged patches over time. It tolerates low fertility, infrequent mowing, and dry shade well, and is frequently blended into northern lawn and roadside seed mixes where its cold tolerance and low input needs are most valuable.

common_name: Champion Bermudagrass (Ultradwarf Putting Green Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish only from sprigs at high density, since Champion is a sterile hybrid with no viable seed; plant in full sun once soil is reliably above 65°F and budget for an intensive grow-in similar to other ultradwarf bermudagrasses.

directions: Establish from densely planted sprigs in full sun once soils are consistently warm, following a topdressing and rolling program similar to other ultradwarf bermudagrasses during grow-in. Champion is an ultradwarf hybrid bermudagrass selected for tolerance of extremely close mowing on golf putting greens, with a reputation among turf managers for good heat tolerance and resistance to spring dead spot compared with some other ultradwarf selections. Its dense, shallow-rooted canopy needs frequent light irrigation, regular verticutting, and a disciplined fertility program to prevent thatch and mat buildup at such a low mowing height. It offers no meaningful shade or wear tolerance for home lawn use and is intended for intensively managed golf greens and tees rather than residential turf.

common_name: SeaDwarf Seashore Paspalum (Fine-Textured Salt-Tolerant Putting Green Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from sprigs or sod after last frost; SeaDwarf is a fine-textured, dwarf seashore paspalum selection bred for close mowing on golf greens while retaining the species' tolerance of saline soil and brackish irrigation water.

directions: Establish from sprigs or sod in full sun once soil is reliably warm, and expect a slower, more carefully managed grow-in than lawn-type seashore paspalum given its finer texture and dwarf habit. SeaDwarf was bred for putting-green and tee use, tolerating mowing heights well below what standard seashore paspalum can handle while keeping the species' exceptional salt tolerance, making it useful where irrigation water is brackish or reclaimed. It needs regular light fertilization and periodic verticutting to manage thatch under its dense growth habit, and performs best with full sun, thinning out in significant shade. Like other seashore paspalum selections it tolerates coastal, salt-affected soils that would exclude bermudagrass or St. Augustine grass, making it valuable for oceanfront golf courses and resort landscapes.
sources: University of Georgia Griffin Campus Turfgrass Research
